prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which established the incretin principle underlying GLP-1-based treatment of diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: All six of us placed B027 first, but that agreement is not the argument; the evidence is. The chain from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect (Holst), through the identification of the biologically active GLP-1(7-36)amide/(7-37) forms (Mojsov), to receptor biology, degradation and the translational path (Drucker) is a coherent physiological discovery that is independently confirmed by large outcome trials and now reaches diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal risk. It combines originality of mechanism with a measurable change in patient outcomes, and the timing is not premature. A single-achievement prize with these three names is the most defensible reading of the credited list, because the discovery lineage is the physiology and the peptide identity, not a particular drug.
statement.case_against: The credited list is imperfect for any three-name cap. Knudsen's design of long-acting analogues (liraglutide, semaglutide) is what actually delivered the medicines, so a prize centred on physiology can look like it honours the biology while leaving out the step that made the therapy work; uncredited early contributors such as Habener also have claims that are hard to dismiss. I also see a real risk that the committee rewards an exceptionally visible clinical story at the expense of mechanistic discoveries that are older and cleaner in attribution, notably the cGAS-STING pathway and the unfolded protein response.

responses.point: Svenningsson proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen for B027, arguing that Knudsen's pharmacological engineering of long-acting analogues is what turned the physiology into drugs, while treating Mojsov's peptide work as a real but secondary contribution.
responses.response: I take the point that the drug-development step is what patients experience, and I would not dismiss it. But I think the Nobel case is for the discovery, and the identification of the active GLP-1 form is the molecular fact on which the pharmacology rests; without it the analogue programme has no defined target to optimise. Knudsen's work is engineering built on that discovery, and Holst and Drucker already cover the physiology and the translational path. I would therefore keep Mojsov over Knudsen, though I accept that this is a judgement about discovery versus development and I would not treat it as settled if the committee wants the prize to reflect the therapy more directly.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks B020 (cGAS-STING) second and regards Chen and Barber as a clean two-person configuration, while calling Knudsen the hardest of the B027 names to fit as a basic-science contributor.
responses.response: I agree on both points and on the B020 attribution: Chen's cGAS and cGAMP work is the decisive biochemical step and Barber's STING is a separable discovery, so two names is defensible, with Ishikawa as the main complication on STING priority. Where I differ is that we both ranked B020 second without testing its main weakness, which is that clinical translation of STING agonists and inhibitors has not yet produced an approved drug. That does not disqualify a mechanism prize, but it makes B020 a strong alternative rather than a competitor to B027 this year.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks optogenetics (B035) second as an invention-type discovery with huge methodological impact, while noting that a three-person cap forces painful exclusions among six credited names.
responses.response: I share the regard for the method, but I am more cautious than he is. The attribution problem is not only the cap: Nagel and Hegemann's characterisation of channelrhodopsin, Bamberg's biophysics and the neuronal deployment by Deisseroth, Boyden and Miesenboeck are separable contributions, and any trio will be contested. The clinical application is also still early. That makes me place B035 below B020 and B043, where the credit is cleaner, but I would not oppose it if the committee is willing to accept a tool prize in physiology.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks B011 (TOR) and would credit only Michael Hall, treating Schreiber's and Sabatini's contributions as more incremental or complicating.
responses.response: I find the single-name argument for Hall reasonable for the genetic identification of TOR, and it avoids the Sabatini dispute. It does leave out the FKBP12-rapamycin target work and the mTORC1 nutrient-sensing chain that made TOR a mammalian physiology story. I ranked B011 below the cGAS-STING and UPR candidates mainly because of that allocation difficulty, so her narrower credit would improve the case for me, but it is a smaller prize than the discovery.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants B027 to honour physiology and peptide identity (Drucker, Holst, Mojsov) or the path to the drugs (including Knudsen); I have not independently verified the priority claims, including those of uncredited early contributors such as Habener.
Whether a three-person B027 prize is better than a two-part prize that pairs the physiology with a second, distinct achievement; the three-person cap makes most such pairings awkward.

Whether B020 (cGAS-STING) or B043 (unfolded protein response) is the better fall-back if B027 is judged too contested on attribution; B020 has the stronger breadth, B043 the cleaner credit and maturity.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I have co-authored with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisen and worked in the same single-cell genomics setting at Karolinska Institutet, but none of the shortlisted candidates or credited names is a documented collaborator, and the unfolded protein response (IRE1-mediated RNA splicing) is close to my RNA-processing interests without any personal tie.
